title: AAROs Supplement To ORNLs Analysis Of A Metallic Specimen
what_is_it: A scientific analysis and historical context document by AARO supplementing Oak Ridge National Laboratory's materials testing of a metallic specimen alleged to be from a crashed extraterrestrial vehicle.
core_summary: AARO and Oak Ridge National Laboratory analyzed a magnesium alloy specimen publicly claimed to be recovered from a 1947 crashed extraterrestrial vehicle with alleged antigravity capabilities. Testing found the specimen's isotopic composition is consistent with terrestrial origin, its elemental structure cannot function as a terahertz waveguide, and its characteristics match well-documented mid-20th century magnesium alloy research and manufacturing processes.
interpretation_warnings: Neither AARO nor ORNL could verify the specimen's historical origin or attribute it to a specific research project.
The specimen's chain of custody is undocumented with unverifiable and conflicting personal accounts.
The specimen has degraded over time (delamination, oxidation) and probably does not represent its original form.
The document is authored by AARO, the same office tasked with resolving anomalous claims, so it is not an independent third-party assessment.
The ORNL analysis summary referenced is a separate document; this supplement provides AARO's concurrence and historical context only.

public_headline: Lab Tests Find Alleged Alien Crash Metal Is Ordinary Terrestrial Alloy
public_tldr: AARO and Oak Ridge National Laboratory tested a magnesium alloy specimen publicly claimed to be debris from a 1947 extraterrestrial vehicle crash. Their analysis found the material's isotopic composition is consistent with terrestrial origin, it cannot function as the terahertz waveguide claimed by proponents, and its properties match mid-20th century magnesium alloy manufacturing.
public_narrative:
The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) published this supplement in July 2024 to accompany Oak Ridge National Laboratory's (ORNL) analysis of a metallic specimen. The specimen — a magnesium alloy — had been publicly alleged to be a component recovered from a crashed extraterrestrial vehicle in 1947, and proponents claimed it could function as a terahertz waveguide capable of generating antigravity effects.

AARO contracted ORNL to conduct materials testing on the specimen. ORNL's findings were straightforward: the magnesium and lead isotopic ratios in the specimen fall within standard terrestrial values. The bismuth in the specimen, which would theoretically need to exist as a pure crystalline layer for any waveguide function, was found to be intermixed with lead — meaning it never existed as the pure layer required for the claimed properties. The specimen's zinc concentration of 1–4% by weight and its columnar magnesium grain structure are consistent with known alloy compositions and manufacturing techniques from that era.

AARO's historical research found that domestic magnesium alloy research began around 1915 and peaked during World War II. The specimen's characteristics — including features consistent with vapor deposition in a vacuum chamber — match what would be expected from a test object, manufacturing byproduct, or aerospace performance study material from mid-20th century research programs. The Falcon GAR-1 air-to-air missile was cited as one example of magnesium alloy use in aerospace applications of that period.

The specimen shows signs of degradation over time, including delamination and oxidation, and AARO concluded it probably does not represent its original configuration, condition, or application. The specimen's chain of custody is undocumented, with unverifiable and conflicting personal accounts complicating any attempt to trace its actual history. Neither AARO nor ORNL could attribute it to a specific research project, in part because failed experiments from that era were rarely documented in detail.
